fiveZipPermits.body:
Montgomery County mechanical permits issued {{p.period_start}} through {{p.period_last}} · ZIPs 20814, 20815, 20816, 20817 and 20895 · County data retrieved {{p.retrieved}}

The finding. Over the year, the county issued {{p.replacements}} mechanical replacement permits for single-family homes and townhouses in these five ZIPs. {{p.described}} of them say what equipment went in. Of those, {{p.hp_any}} ({{p.hp_any_described_share}}%) name a heat pump, and {{p.fossil_no_hp}} ({{p.fossil_no_hp_described_share}}%) name a furnace or boiler with no heat pump. Just {{p.switch}} spell out a switch from a gas furnace to a heat pump. Census estimates say utility gas heats about {{p.fuel_total.gas_share}}% of occupied homes in these ZIPs.

What the permit descriptions say

Every county mechanical permit carries a short description, written by whoever applied for it. We sorted each residential replacement into one row of the table below. A permit goes to the first row whose wording it matches, working from the top. The exact rules are under Method.

{{TABLE:p_buckets}}

Four things stand out.

  • A furnace and an AC together is the most common job that names its equipment, with {{p.fossil_and_ac}} permits. Another {{p.fossil_only}} name a furnace or boiler with no AC.
  • Heat pumps appear in four forms. {{p.hp_only}} name a heat pump with no furnace or boiler, {{p.hp_and_fossil}} name a heat pump and a furnace or boiler together, {{p.hybrid}} use hybrid or dual-fuel wording, and {{p.switch}} describe a switch away from a gas furnace. A further {{p.ductless}} name ductless or mini-split equipment.
  • {{p.ac_only}} permits name an AC and no heating equipment. These are the jobs where the cooling side was replaced and the heating side, as far as the permit says, was left alone.
  • {{p.no_detail}} permits ({{p.no_detail_share}}%) carry no equipment detail at all. The description is blank, or holds only a form phrase or a reference number. Any share in this report could move if those permits were described.

When the work happened

The season shows up in the descriptions. {{p.ac_in_season}} of the {{p.ac_only}} AC-only replacements ({{p.ac_in_season_share}}%) were issued April through July. Furnace-only replacements ran the other way: {{p.fossil_only_winter}} of {{p.fossil_only}} ({{p.fossil_only_winter_share}}%) were issued November through March.

{{TABLE:p_monthly}}

How homes in these ZIPs heat

The Census Bureau’s American Community Survey asks households what fuel heats their home. Across these five ZIPs, an estimated {{p.fuel_total.gas}} of {{p.fuel_total.homes}} occupied homes ({{p.fuel_total.gas_share}}%) heat with utility gas, and {{p.fuel_total.electric}} ({{p.fuel_total.electric_share}}%) with electricity. The gas share runs from {{p.fuel.0.gas_share}}% in 20814 to {{p.fuel.4.gas_share}}% in 20895.

{{TABLE:p_fuel}}

Read the two sources together with care. The Census figures cover every occupied home, including apartments and condominiums, while the permits in this report are houses and townhouses. The estimates are a 2020 to 2024 average, not a 2026 count. Electric heat in a home can mean a heat pump or electric resistance heat; the survey doesn’t say which.

What the permits can’t tell us

  • Why the work happened. A permit doesn’t say whether the old system failed, the owner planned an upgrade, or the house was being remodeled or sold.
  • What the homeowner was offered. We see what was permitted, not the options that were quoted and turned down.
  • Price, financing or rebates. None of these are in the county data.
  • Whether a heat pump and a furnace on one permit are one system. Some of those {{p.hp_and_fossil}} descriptions are a dual-fuel setup; others describe two separate systems in one house, such as an attic heat pump and a basement furnace.
  • Whether the house kept its gas service.
  • How many homes this is. One house can have more than one permit, and one permit can cover several systems.
  • Work done without a permit. It doesn’t appear here.

This report also leaves out lead costs, close rates and comparisons between named companies. We’ll publish those only when we have data we can cite.

What we still need to learn

The permits show what was installed. The next part has to come from the people involved.

From contractors: When the AC fails and the furnace still works, which options do you put in front of the homeowner? How often is each one chosen? What rules out a heat pump most often: the electrical panel, the price, the furnace’s age, or worry about comfort in the cold?

From homeowners: What were you offered? What did you choose, and why? Did anyone lay the options out in writing?

If you can answer any of these, write to max@maxfisher.net. When we have enough answers to report, we’ll publish them as counts, with the number of responses and the gaps in who answered.

Method

We downloaded every record in the county’s Mechanical Permits dataset with an issue date from {{p.period_start}} through {{p.period_last}} and one of the five ZIP codes: {{p.all}} permits. Our download matched the county’s own count for each ZIP. {{p.residential}} are for single-family dwellings or townhouses. Of those, {{p.replacements}} have the work type “Replace” and are the subject of this report. The other {{p.residential_install}} have the work type “Install,” which takes in new houses and additions as well as equipment, so we kept them out of the replacement counts.

Each description is lowercased and checked against these rows in order. The first match wins:

{{TABLE:p_rules}}

The rules are simple keyword matches, so they can be checked by hand. We read samples from every row to test them; typos and unusual wording will still put some permits in the wrong row. The classification script is part of this publication’s source files.

An earlier classified file we worked from listed {{p.earlier_file_rows}} permits for the same ZIPs and dates. We couldn’t reproduce which county records it left out, so this report starts again from the county’s full export.

Sources

  • Montgomery County Department of Permitting Services, Mechanical Permits. Retrieved {{p.sources.permits.retrieved_utc}}; county rows last updated {{p.sources.permits.rows_updated_utc}}. SHA-256 of our export: {{p.sources.permits.sha256}}.
  • U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020–2024 5-year estimates, table B25040, House Heating Fuel, for ZIP Code Tabulation Areas 20814, 20815, 20816, 20817 and 20895. Retrieved {{p.sources.acs.retrieved_utc}} through Census Reporter, which republishes the Bureau’s tables. SHA-256: {{p.sources.acs.sha256}}.

acFailsFurnaceWorks.body:
For owners, comfort advisors and service techs · Montgomery County, Maryland · Figures from the five-ZIP permit report

The short version. Name all three options, in the same order, every time: replace the AC, put in a heat pump that works with the furnace, or switch fully to a heat pump. For each one, say what it replaces, what it keeps, and what you have to check before you can quote it. Then let the homeowner choose.

Why this call matters here

In our five-ZIP permit report, {{p.ac_only}} residential replacement permits over the past year named an AC and no heating equipment, and {{p.ac_in_season_share}}% of them were issued April through July. Census estimates say utility gas heats about {{p.fuel_total.gas_share}}% of occupied homes in those ZIPs. Put together, that’s the common call: the AC quit in the heat, and a gas furnace that still runs sits in the basement.

It’s also the call where the homeowner has the least time to think. If only one option comes up, it’s usually the AC. Laying out all three takes a few extra minutes, and the homeowner leaves knowing what they chose and why.

Ask three questions before any price

  1. How old is the furnace, and has it given trouble? Read the data plate. Don’t guess.
  2. How long do they plan to stay in the house?
  3. What bothers them now? A hot or cold room, the gas bill, noise, a remodel coming up.

The answers tell you which option to describe in the most detail. You still describe all three.

The three options, side by side

Option1. New AC2. Heat pump with furnace backup3. Full switch to a heat pump
What gets replacedThe outdoor AC, and usually the indoor coil.The AC becomes a heat pump. New coil, and a thermostat or control that runs both systems.The AC becomes a heat pump. The furnace is replaced by an air handler with electric backup heat.
What staysThe furnace, the ducts and the gas service.The furnace, as backup heat for the coldest hours. The ducts and the gas service.The ducts, if they’re sized for it. Gas can stay for other appliances.
Check before you quoteThe coil matches the furnace’s blower and cabinet. The condition of the refrigerant lines. The furnace’s age.How the controls decide when the furnace takes over. That the furnace works with the new coil. That the homeowner knows which system heats when.A room-by-room load calculation (Manual J). Panel and circuit capacity for the air handler and backup heat. Duct size and airflow. Heat pump output at your local design temperature.
Often fits whenThe furnace is fairly new and the homeowner wants the smallest change.The furnace has years left and the homeowner wants to burn less gas without giving it up.The furnace is near the end of its life too, and the homeowner wants one system and less gas, or none.

How to say it

Keep it short and keep the order. Something like this:

“Your AC needs replacing, and your furnace still works. So you have three ways to go. One: we replace just the AC, and you keep heating with gas like you do today. Two: we put in a heat pump instead of an AC. It cools the same way, and it also heats the house for most of the winter, with your furnace taking over when it’s coldest. Three: we replace both with a heat pump system and retire the furnace. I’ll write down what each one includes, what I’d need to check, and the price, and you decide.”

Put it in writing

One page, three columns, the same order you used out loud. For each option, list:

  • The equipment and its size
  • What stays in place
  • What has to be checked or upgraded first, such as the panel, the ducts or the controls
  • The price, the warranty and how long the work takes

If you mention a rebate, write the program’s name and the date you checked it. Program rules and deadlines change.

What not to do

  • Don’t present one option and bring up the others only if you’re asked.
  • Don’t promise a savings number you can’t show the math for. Operating cost depends on gas and electric rates, the equipment, the house and how the homeowner runs it.
  • Don’t call the furnace unsafe without a test result to show.
  • Don’t size the new equipment by the old unit’s tonnage alone.

What we don’t know yet

We don’t yet know how often local homeowners pick each option, or what tips the decision. The permits show the result in only some of the jobs: {{p.hybrid}} use hybrid or dual-fuel wording, {{p.hp_and_fossil}} name a heat pump and a furnace or boiler together, and {{p.switch}} spell out a full switch. If you have this conversation often, tell us what you see at max@maxfisher.net. We’ll report the answers as counts, with the number of responses.

about.title: About Embrace Insight
about.description: Embrace Insight is an independent publication for Montgomery County HVAC owners: local market reports from public records and practical guides for the decisions owners face on the next call.
about.author: Max Fisher
about.body:
Local reporting and practical guides for Montgomery County HVAC owners. Embrace Insight is an independent publication by Max Fisher. It isn’t a government site, a contractor or a lead service.

What we publish

  • Market Reports use public records, such as county permits and Census estimates, to show what is happening in specific ZIP codes. Each one lists its sources, retrieval dates and limits.
  • Contractor Playbook guides take a decision owners face on real calls and lay out a simple way to explain it to a homeowner.

What we don’t publish

No rankings, no lead lists and no comparisons between named companies. No lead costs or close rates until we have data we can cite. When a question can’t be answered from the record, we say so.

How we work

Official sources, linked. Observations, calculations and estimates labeled. Retrieval dates visible. Unknowns stay unknown. The full editorial standard explains how we handle sources and corrections.

Contact

Corrections, data and story ideas: max@maxfisher.net. There’s no email list yet; when there is, signing up will be a separate, clear choice.

Homeowners looking for rebate and heat pump guidance can use our companion resource, DMV Heat Pumps.

briefing20814.title: In 20814, the county marks 66 of 138 buildings “No.”
briefing20814.description: What Montgomery County’s BEPS inventory and energy performance map show for ZIP 20814 as of November 7, 2026: projected interim standard readings by building type, coverage gaps, and an October permits comparison.
briefing20814.author: Max Fisher
briefing20814.body:
County exports retrieved November 7, 2026 · ZIP {{zip}} · Montgomery County, Maryland · Energy map reporting-year label, as published: {{reporting_year_label}}

The finding. Montgomery County’s energy performance map lists {{interim.no}} of the {{matched}} matched buildings in ZIP {{zip}} as not meeting their projected interim performance standard. {{interim.yes}} read Yes and {{interim.undisclosed}} read Undisclosed. Hotels ({{use.hotel.no}} of {{use.hotel.records}}) and multifamily housing ({{use.multifamily housing.no}} of {{use.multifamily housing.records}}) account for most of the No readings. Offices run the other way: {{use.office.yes}} of {{use.office.records}} read Yes.

What it can inform

The county publishes a projection for each building it tracks. Where one building type sits mostly on the “No” side, that type is where the county’s own figures put the most distance between published energy use and the interim standard. For an HVAC business that serves, or wants to serve, larger buildings in {{zip}}, that makes it the building type to understand first: how those buildings are typically heated and cooled, who makes system decisions, and what the county’s rules ask of them.

The decision it can inform: which building type to study first, and which questions to bring to that conversation. It cannot tell you which building to call.

By building type

Matched records only. Use types from the county inventory; readings from the energy map’s “Meeting Interim Standard” field.

{{TABLE:by_use}}

Against the projected final standard, the split widens: {{final.no}} read No, {{final.yes}} read Yes, and {{final.undisclosed}} read Undisclosed.

How to read the columns

The map carries a “Benchmarking Report Status” column and separate “Meeting Interim Standard” and “Meeting Final Standard” columns. The first tracks whether a building’s benchmarking report was filed and accepted. The standard columns compare the building’s published energy use with its projected targets. {{interim_no_and_report_in_compliance}} of the {{interim.no}} buildings that read No for the interim standard read “in compliance” for benchmarking report status. Read each column on its own terms. Neither one is a compliance determination by Embrace Insight.

Coverage and gaps

  • {{inventory_in_zip}} inventory records and {{energy_in_zip}} energy map records list postal code {{zip}}. All {{matched}} energy map records matched an inventory record by exact county building ID.
  • {{unmatched_count}} inventory records have no energy map match: two multifamily buildings (named “Cecil” and “Hampden House” in the inventory) and one record with no name or use type.
  • Among matched records, {{eui_blank}} have a blank normalized net site EUI and {{eui_undisclosed}} read “Undisclosed.” Both Undisclosed interim readings are multifamily buildings.
  • ZIP comes from the county’s published postal code. We did not assign ZIPs from street addresses. Two records elsewhere in the export carry invalid postal codes and are outside this scope.
  • The reporting-year label ({{reporting_year_label}}) is the county’s. We have not mapped it to a calendar year of energy use.

What it does not show

Equipment type, age, or condition. An owner’s plans, budget, or timeline. Whether a building qualifies for an exemption or will pursue an alternative pathway. Any project, bid, or purchase. Confirm the building record and the county’s current requirements before relying on any value.

The permits comparison

The county’s Mechanical Permits dataset lists {{permits.county}} permits with October 2026 issue dates; the latest issue date in the data is {{permits.last_issue_date}}, and the source last reported a row update on October 30. {{permits.zip}} list ZIP {{zip}}: {{permits.worktype.REPLACE}} replacements and {{permits.worktype.INSTALL}} installs, covering {{permits.usecode.SINGLE FAMILY DWELLING}} single-family dwellings, {{permits.usecode.TOWNHOUSE}} townhouses, and {{permits.usecode.BUSINESS BUILDING}} business buildings. That is recorded permitting activity, mostly residential, and a different population from the BEPS buildings above. City permit systems are outside the dataset, and a permit does not confirm the equipment type or completed work.

Method

  1. Downloaded the county BEPS building inventory and the energy performance map with their official export controls on November 7, 2026, and recorded each file’s SHA-256 checksum.
  2. Kept records whose published postal code is {{zip}}.
  3. Joined the two exports on exact county building ID. No name-based or fuzzy matching.
  4. Kept every published value as text, including blanks and “Undisclosed,” and counted directly from those values.
  5. Queried the county Mechanical Permits API for October issue dates and confirmed the download matched an independent count query. A recheck on November 7 returned the same {{permits.county}} records.

Sources

  • Montgomery County BEPS building inventory. Export file time {{sources.inventory.file_time_utc}}; SHA-256 {{sources.inventory.sha256}}.
  • Montgomery County energy performance map. Export file time {{sources.energy.file_time_utc}}; SHA-256 {{sources.energy.sha256}}.
  • Montgomery County Mechanical Permits dataset. Retrieved {{sources.permits.retrieved_utc}}.
  • Montgomery County BEPS scope announcement.

Every building-level value is in the 20814 BEPS Data Sheet. Send a correction or a source to max@maxfisher.net.

rebates.title: A rebate headline is not an approval.
rebates.description: A source-checked starting point for DMV heat pump rebates, program timing, and tax-credit questions.
rebates.author: Max Fisher
rebates.body:
A national incentive headline is a starting point. Your address, utility, household, equipment, and project timing determine which program rules you need to read. A program cap is not an award for your home.

DC: identify the program route

DOEE directs federally funded home-energy assistance through AHEP and AHRA. It describes DCSEU residential rebates as a separate route. Check the specific program before comparing offers. Read DOEE’s program explanation ↗

Maryland: distinguish a proposed launch from an open application

MEA’s September 30, 2026 update says revised federal rebate applications were submitted and launch depends on DOE approval. This does not establish access to a federal rebate today. Separate utility offers need their own review. Check MEA’s current status ↗

Virginia: use the current FAQ

Virginia Energy’s October 13, 2026 FAQ says its federal Home Energy Rebates are not yet available. Final access procedures and launch timing remain unsettled. Ask about existing alternatives through the agency’s links. Read Virginia Energy’s FAQ ↗

Rebates and tax credits are different

Do not carry old tax-credit copy into a 2026 budget. The IRS describes the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit for improvements made through December 31, 2025. That is not a promised credit for a new 2026 installation. Check the IRS timing rules ↗

Five checks before a purchase

  1. Confirm your service address and electric utility.
  2. Identify the exact program and its administrator.
  3. Ask whether preapproval, an assessment, or a participating contractor is required.
  4. Get written confirmation of qualifying equipment, timing, documentation, and payment process.
  5. Keep the dated program terms alongside your quote.

These are research steps, not an eligibility determination. Recheck the official program when making a decision; this briefing is a dated snapshot.

beps.title: BEPS starts with the building.
beps.description: How DMV residents and condo owners can start checking building-performance coverage and responsibilities.
beps.author: Max Fisher
beps.body:
Building Energy Performance Standards, or BEPS, concern the performance of covered buildings. Start with the building and jurisdiction, then establish who is responsible for the records. A regional headline cannot establish your home’s obligations.

Maryland and Montgomery County are distinct programs

MDE identifies commercial and multifamily buildings of at least 35,000 square feet for its state program, subject to exemption procedures. Montgomery County describes its local BEPS program as covering most commercial and multifamily buildings of at least 25,000 square feet. These thresholds are a screening step, not a final determination. Maryland program ↗ · County scope and adopted regulation ↗

DC has its own program

DOEE maintains DC’s BEPS program and directs readers to its current building-energy portal. Use that jurisdiction’s records and guidance to establish coverage and applicable requirements. Start with DC DOEE ↗

If you own a condo or rent

Ask the association or building manager which building record applies, whether coverage has been confirmed, who manages benchmarking, and where the current plan and deadlines are recorded. A unit owner’s decisions and whole-building responsibilities can be different.

What a performance gap does not establish

A disclosed energy metric or a gap to a future target does not by itself prove current noncompliance, identify required HVAC work, or establish a project budget. Check reporting status, applicable deadlines, approved pathways, and official correspondence before drawing that conclusion.

A useful next conversation

Bring your building address, jurisdiction, building ID if available, current reporting record, and questions to the program administrator or your qualified adviser. This is an educational starting point, not legal advice, a compliance certification, or an engineering assessment.

planning.title: Look past the heat pump price tag.
planning.description: Questions to ask before comparing heat pump proposals and relying on a potential rebate.
planning.author: Max Fisher
planning.body:
A useful heat pump conversation starts with your home and the scope of work. Keep equipment choices, home conditions, incentives, and installation responsibilities in the same record so you can compare like with like.

Describe the home before comparing prices

Record your current heating and cooling equipment, its age if known, the rooms that are uncomfortable, and the upgrades you are considering. Ask the contractor how the proposal accounts for your home’s heating and cooling needs. Keep model numbers and assumptions in the quote.

Ask what is included

Ask about the assessment, electrical and duct work, controls, permits, removal of old equipment, commissioning, warranty, and service arrangements. Identify exclusions and who is responsible for each step. These questions help define a scope; this worksheet does not size or design your system.

Resolve program requirements before relying on a discount

Some programs require an assessment or a particular contractor process. Virginia’s current FAQ, for example, describes assessment requirements in its proposed federal programs and warns against assuming a project will qualify before launch. Read the program’s own requirements ↗

Use a decision record

For each proposal, write down the cash price, separately identified potential incentive, who applies, what evidence is needed, and whether approval is confirmed or pending. Ask how a funding delay or rejection would affect your payment obligation.

Keep the next step practical

Use the Quote Companion to collect answers. Confirm the program terms with the administrator and technical scope with a qualified contractor before making a commitment. No savings, rebate eligibility, or particular equipment outcome is guaranteed by this guide.

privacy.title: Your email. A clear choice.
privacy.body:
Embrace Insight is an independent publication for Montgomery County home service businesses. The site stores resource requests and email signup choices.

What is recorded

Your email address, request type, requested asset, signup source, supplied campaign tags, timestamp, and the consent wording/version are stored. Historical clearance requests, if submitted through a retained link, also store a public page URL and target query. Do not enter private signed links or credentials. Short-lived hashed request markers help limit abuse; raw network addresses are not stored in the contact list.

Resources and newsletter are separate

Entering your email for a resource records that request and gives you a download link. It does not request the newsletter unless you choose the separate checkbox. Standalone newsletter signup requires an explicit choice. Repeated requests use one contact record while retaining distinct request and consent events.

Confirmation and delivery

Newsletter requests remain pending email confirmation. This private preview does not send confirmation emails or newsletters automatically. An email delivery platform has not yet been connected. Download access is available immediately after a successful saved request.

Your preferences

A private preference link is shown after each successful request. Use it to withdraw newsletter signup or mark the address unsubscribed. Opening that link alone does not change preferences; the form requires a deliberate confirmation. For access, correction, or removal requests, contact max@maxfisher.net.

Access and storage

The site uses Sites hosting with a private D1 database. Contact records and exports are restricted to the publisher. Test addresses ending in .invalid are excluded from the real-list exports. The hosting provider may process technical information to deliver and protect the site. External source sites have their own practices.

Before public launch

Final privacy terms, retention rules, the email confirmation/delivery workflow, editorial review, and the actual public page’s six-gate validation require completion. Subscriber data is not part of an unrestricted research or RAG corpus.

editorial.title: The source comes with the story.
editorial.description: Our approach to sources, dated program information, corrections, and independence.
editorial.author: Max Fisher
editorial.body:
Embrace Insight is an independent publication for HVAC owners and operators in Maryland, starting in Montgomery County. We report what public records show (building energy filings, permits, and other attributable sources) and keep source observations, our calculations, and estimates labeled separately.

What insider insight means here

We read program details, explain the differences between jurisdictions, and connect those details to practical questions. We do not claim privileged government access, official agency status, or access to unannounced funding.

Sources and dates

Time-sensitive statements link to the responsible agency or program. A source-checked date records when we reviewed that information. It is not a promise that the information remains unchanged or that the page updates automatically.

Evidence and interpretation

Program status, quoted rules, and our interpretation are kept distinct. Missing information stays unknown. A program headline does not establish household eligibility; a building’s performance data does not by itself establish noncompliance.

Corrections and responsibility

Max Fisher is the responsible publisher. Send a source, a correction, or a question to max@maxfisher.net. Material corrections should identify what changed and when. No government endorsement or installation service is claimed.

Commercial relationships

Any future paid placement, affiliate link, or referral relationship must be clearly identified where it appears. This draft does not present a paid contractor directory or endorse a provider. The separate SEO agency is outside this publication’s resident-facing offer.

Publishing quality

Semantic Gate remains our internal six-gate release requirement for the final public URL and target query. This owner-private draft is not publicly certified. It retains private access and indexing restrictions pending launch review.
